body_html:
White label reporting means delivering client reports under your agency's brand, even when a partner does the work or builds the dashboards. Done well, it shows clients a clear story: results first, then visibility, rankings, and the work completed, all in your logo, colors, and voice.

If you resell SEO, PPC, or social services, the report is often the only part of the work your client actually sees each month. It carries your reputation. This guide covers what to include, how to brand it, how to handle data access, and the mistakes that make white label reports feel generic.

What is white label reporting?

In a white label arrangement, a partner agency or freelancer handles part of the delivery, and you present it as your own. White label reporting extends that to the reports: the dashboards, PDFs, or decks your client receives carry only your branding. There's no partner logo, no unfamiliar email address, and no tool watermarks that point somewhere else.

That doesn't mean hiding the truth about results. The numbers come straight from the client's own accounts, such as Google Search Console, GA4, or Google Ads. Only the presentation is yours.

What should a white label report show clients?

Clients don't want more data. They want to know whether the money they spend with you is working. Build every report around that, in this order:

  1. A short written summary. What changed this period, why, and what's next. Three to five sentences in plain language.
  2. Business outcomes. Leads, calls, bookings, or sales from the channels you manage. In GA4, these are the actions marked as key events.
  3. Channel performance. For SEO: clicks, impressions, CTR, and average position from Search Console. For paid search: spend, conversions, and cost per conversion. For social: reach and engagement tied to clicks or leads.
  4. Priority keywords or campaigns. A focused set, grouped by service or theme, with movement since last period.
  5. Health checks. Indexing issues, Core Web Vitals, broken tracking, or ad disapprovals. One line each unless something needs attention.
  6. Work completed and next steps. What was delivered and what's planned. This is where the partner's work becomes visible to the client, under your name.

Keep comparisons consistent. Show the current period against the previous period and, for seasonal businesses, the same period last year. Without that context, a normal seasonal dip reads like a failure.

What to leave out

  • Tool-specific scores that clients can't act on, unless you explain them.
  • Raw keyword dumps of hundreds of rows. Move them to an appendix if a client asks for them.
  • Internal notes meant for your partner, like task IDs or production comments.
  • Metrics that change every month. Pick a set and stick with it, so clients can compare progress over time.

How to brand a white label report

Branding is more than swapping a logo. A client should feel the report came from the same team they talk to on calls.

Visual branding

Use your logo, brand colors, and fonts across every page. If you build reports in Data Studio, Google's free dashboard tool (called Looker Studio until its rename back to Data Studio in 2026), you can set a report theme for colors and fonts. Its theme settings can even generate a color palette from an image, so text and chart colors can match your logo. Custom themes don't carry from one report to the next, so build one branded template and copy it for each client.

Delivery branding

The report should arrive from you. That means:

  • Emails sent from your domain or your team's addresses, not a partner's.
  • Shared dashboards owned by an account your agency controls.
  • File names, page titles, and footers that use your agency name.
  • Your contact details on the report, so questions come to you.

Data Studio can email a PDF of the report on a schedule, with a link back to the live version. Set the schedule from an account your agency owns so the delivery comes from you. The free edition allows one schedule per report and a daily maximum frequency; the Pro edition raises those limits.

Voice branding

The written summary is where most white label reports give themselves away. Generic text that reads the same for every client tells them nobody looked closely. Write the summary in your agency's voice, mention the client's own goals, and connect the numbers to decisions you've discussed with them. If your partner drafts it, edit it before it goes out.

How should agencies handle data access for white label reporting?

Access is where white label setups often get messy. A few rules keep it clean and safe.

The client should own their accounts. Search Console, GA4, Google Business Profile, and ad accounts belong to the client's business. Your agency gets access, and your partner gets access through you. If the relationship ends, the client keeps their data.

Give partners the least access they need. Search Console has three permission levels: owner, full user, and restricted user. According to Google's help page on managing Search Console owners, users, and permissions, restricted users can view most data but can't take actions like submitting sitemaps. For reporting alone, that's often enough. Apply the same thinking in GA4 and ad platforms.

Keep a simple access log. List which accounts each client has, who has access, and at what level. Review it when a partner or employee changes.

Which tools work for white label reporting?

You can start with free tools and add paid ones as your client list grows. Common options include:

  • Data Studio: connects directly to Search Console, GA4, and Google Ads, with custom themes and scheduled email delivery.
  • SEO platforms: tools like Semrush and Ahrefs include rank tracking and report builders with options for adding your own branding, depending on the plan.
  • Slides or documents: useful for quarterly reviews, where commentary matters more than live data.

Whatever you choose, aim for one consistent template across clients. It's faster to produce, easier to check, and makes onboarding a new client a matter of connecting data sources rather than designing from scratch. If you'd rather not build and maintain that template yourself, custom white label reporting dashboards can be set up under your brand.

Common white label reporting mistakes

  • Leaving traces of the partner. A stray logo, an unfamiliar sender, or a dashboard URL owned by someone else raises questions you don't want to answer mid-campaign.
  • Reporting activity instead of results. "We published four posts" matters less than what those posts did for leads.
  • Skipping quality checks. Broken charts or date ranges that don't match make your agency look careless, even if the partner made the error. Review every report before it goes out.
  • Hiding bad months. Explain drops honestly, with a likely cause and a plan. Clients forgive dips far more readily than surprises.
  • Overpromising in the summary. Never imply guaranteed rankings or traffic. Report what happened and what you're doing next.

Frequently asked questions

Is white label reporting honest?

Yes, as long as the data is real and unedited. White labeling changes who presents the work, not what the work achieved. Your agency is still responsible for the results, the strategy, and the client relationship. The numbers should come directly from the client's own accounts, and the written summary should describe them accurately, including the months that don't go well. Some agencies also mention to clients that they work with specialist partners.

How often should agencies send white label reports?

Monthly reporting suits most SEO and social clients, since those channels change gradually. Paid search clients with larger budgets may want a live dashboard they can check any time, plus a monthly summary. Add a quarterly review for every client to step back and look at trends together. Whatever schedule you choose, keep it consistent so the report becomes a dependable part of your service.

Who should write the summary in a white label report?

Whoever writes the first draft, someone at your agency should finish it. Your partner may know the data best, but you know the client: their goals, worries, and what you promised on the last call. Have the partner send a draft with key findings, then edit it into your own voice and add client-specific context. That final pass is what makes the report feel personal rather than templated.

Can clients see where the report data comes from?

They should be able to. Showing data sources, such as Search Console, GA4, or Google Ads, builds trust because clients can check the numbers in their own accounts. White label reporting removes the partner's branding, not the source of the data. Label each section with its source and date range, and give clients access to their own accounts so they never depend on you just to see their numbers.
